claims.text: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi contains approximately 20 at.% each of Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, and Ti.
Homogenization minimizes large intermetallic precipitates and prior substructure in CoCrFeNiTi.
Local chemical inhomogeneities and short-range order in CoCrFeNiTi reduce the net lattice-friction stress.
Local chemical inhomogeneities and short-range order maintain active dislocation pathways in CoCrFeNiTi.
The combination of reduced lattice friction and active dislocation pathways produces moderate hardness and strength together with notable ductility in CoCrFeNiTi.
Other high-entropy alloys dominated by harder intermetallic phases are more brittle than the proposed CoCrFeNiTi solid solution.
Tailored annealing or minor compositional changes can introduce controlled short-range order without causing bulk precipitation.
The hypothesis is limited to single-phase, FCC-like or BCC-like CoCrFeNiTi solid solutions tested at 25 °C or 600 °C at approximately 10^-3 s^-1.
Short-range ordering produces local chemically ordered nanodomains that intermittently pin and guide dislocations.
Partially ordered clusters increase lattice friction.
The increase in lattice friction caused by partially ordered clusters raises hardness and strength modestly.
Partially ordered clusters leave enough dislocation mobility to retain macroscopic ductility.
Relative to fully homogenized CoCrFeNiTi, controlled short-range order will increase hardness by tens of HV.
Relative to fully homogenized CoCrFeNiTi, controlled short-range order will increase yield strength by approximately 10–30%.
Short-range-ordered CoCrFeNiTi will preserve more than approximately 5–10% plastic strain under the specified test conditions.
The homogenized CoCrFeNiTi baseline has hardness of approximately 200–400 HV, yield strength in the hundreds of MPa, and plasticity above approximately 5–10% elongation.
Significant intermetallic precipitation or large secondary-phase fractions shift the dominant strengthening mechanism away from short-range ordering.
Direct atomic-scale evidence connecting short-range order to mechanical response in CoCrFeNiTi is sparse.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis says short-range ordering reduces net lattice-friction stress, whereas the mechanism says partially ordered clusters elevate lattice friction to increase hardness and strength.
